screens.title: Configuring Basic BGP Peering and Route Advertisement
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn the practical steps to bring BGP peering online and to advertise prefixes so routers exchange reachability information. We begin with the single global command that starts BGP — the router bgp command — and then configure both eBGP, which peers across different Autonomous Systems, and iBGP, which peers inside the same ASN using loopback addresses for stability. You will also learn the network command’s exact-match requirement for advertising prefixes and why an underlying route in the IP routing table matters. Finally, we cover the essential show commands you will run to verify neighbor state, seen prefixes, and what is advertised to each peer. These tasks matter because BGP is the control plane for exchanging routes between domains; small mistakes like a missing update-source or a wrong mask stop route propagation and can cause outages. As you move through the screens you’ll see configuration snippets and a step-by-step lab topology you can recreate in your simulator. Keep an eye on common mistakes such as blocked TCP port 179 and accidentally advertising private address space. By the end you should be able to form basic eBGP and iBGP sessions and verify their operation with confidence.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Introduction
Configuring Basic BGP Peering
From router bgp to neighbor commands — what you must know to form sessions and advertise routes.
In this lesson
eBGP and iBGP peering, network command exact match, verification commands.
Why it matters
BGP controls cross-domain reachability; correct peering and advertisements prevent outages and route leaks.
Safety note
Avoid advertising RFC1918 ranges to eBGP peers. Use filters and verify advertised-routes before committing changes.
Explore Key Topics
eBGP Peering
Direct ASN-to-ASN peering; neighbor remote-as and TCP 179.
iBGP over Loopbacks
Use update-source Loopback0 and ensure IGP reachability to loopbacks.
Network Injection
network requires an exact route in the routing table before BGP will advertise it.
Topology Preview
R1 (AS65001) peers eBGP with R2 (AS65002) and iBGP with R3 (AS65001) over loopbacks. OSPF provides reachability between loopbacks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on the hands-on skills you will practice and the reasons they matter in production networks. First, you will configure basic eBGP peering between two directly connected routers in different Autonomous Systems — this demonstrates the neighbor remote-as pattern and the reliance on TCP port 179 for session establishment. Second, you will configure iBGP peering between routers in the same ASN using loopback interfaces and the update-source command; this gives greater session stability because loopbacks remain reachable as long as the IGP can route to them. Third, you will advertise network prefixes into BGP using the network command and learn the requirement that the exact prefix and mask must already exist in the router’s IP routing table — a common stumbling block for learners. Fourth, you will verify BGP neighbor status and route exchange using show ip bgp summary, show ip bgp, and show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. Each of these skills is practical: they let you bring up sessions reliably, avoid accidental route leakage, and confirm what your router sends and receives before you make irreversible changes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Focus
screens.narratorSegment: Now we translate objectives into the exact actions you will take in the lab and on real routers. For eBGP you will enter router bgp with the local ASN and then add neighbor remote-as ; success requires TCP reachability to port 179 and matching remote-as on the far side. For iBGP you will configure neighbor loopback-ip remote-as local-as and add neighbor loopback-ip update-source Loopback0; this tells the router to source the TCP connection from the loopback address so peers recognize the expected source. When advertising networks, you will use network prefix mask netmask, but only after you ensure that prefix exists in the routing table — for example a loopback with an IP in that prefix or a static route pointing to null0 for summaries. For verification you will rely on show ip bgp summary to confirm Established state, show ip bgp to view the BGP table contents, and show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes to confirm what you are sending. Each of these steps reduces risk: proper sourcing, reachability, and verification prevent broken sessions and accidental route leaks.

screens.title: Starting BGP: router bgp and the ASN
screens.narratorSegment: The foundation of any BGP configuration is the simple global command router bgp followed by your Autonomous System Number, or ASN. This command tells the router to start the BGP process and to identify itself in BGP OPEN messages with that ASN. Think of the ASN like the administrative domain label: routers with different ASNs form eBGP sessions, while routers that share the same ASN form iBGP sessions. A concrete example is router bgp 65001 on R1 when R1 is managed as ASN 65001. That single command switches the device into BGP mode and lets you begin configuring neighbor relationships and route advertisements. A common misconception is that configuring router bgp alone advertises routes; it does not. You still must advertise specific prefixes or redistribute routes into BGP before those networks are shared with peers. Another subtle point is that ASNs must be correct on both ends of a peer relationship: a wrong remote-as prevents the session from ever reaching Established. Key takeaway: router bgp enables the process and identifies your domain. Always pair it with explicit neighbor definitions and verification steps so you know the process has established successfully.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: router bgp <ASN> starts the BGP process and sets the router's Autonomous System Number used in peer negotiations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Starting BGP
router bgp & ASN
Start BGP by assigning the router's Autonomous System Number; this determines eBGP vs iBGP relationships.
Concept

The ASN identifies the administrative domain. Routers use it during the BGP OPEN handshake.

Common misconception
Enabling router bgp does not advertise routes by itself. You must use the network command or redistribution to originate prefixes into BGP.
Key Takeaway

Use router bgp to begin BGP configuration; always follow with neighbor and advertisement configuration and verification.

Concrete Example
! On R1
router bgp 65001
If R1 and R2 are in different ASNs, add neighbor lines to form eBGP. If two routers share ASN 65001, they behave as iBGP peers unless other settings change.
Check
After configuring router bgp and neighbors, use show ip bgp summary to confirm the process is present and neighbors progress toward Established.

screens.title: Configuring eBGP Peering
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring eBGP is straightforward but requires precise addressing and the correct remote ASN. To form an eBGP session between directly connected routers you configure router bgp with your local ASN and then define neighbor remote-as. For example, on R1 in AS 65001 you add neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002; on R2 you add neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote-as 65001. BGP uses TCP port 179 to build the session; if TCP is blocked by an ACL or firewall the neighbor will stay in Active. Another important point: eBGP peers often use directly connected IP addresses for the neighbor statement, so underlying interface IP reachability is necessary. When peers are separated by multiple hops, ebgp-multihop can be used to increase TTL, for example neighbor 192.168.1.2 ebgp-multihop 2, but use this deliberately because it changes how BGP packets traverse the network. Concrete example: configure the neighbor commands on both routers, then verify with show ip bgp summary to see an Established session and the number of prefixes exchanged. Misconception to avoid: eBGP is not automatic when routers can ping each other; the neighbor remote-as must match and control-plane TCP must be allowed. Takeaway: set the correct remote-as and confirm TCP reachability before troubleshooting deeper.

keyIdea.text: neighbor <IP> remote-as <ASN> defines an eBGP peer; ensure TCP 179 reachability and correct ASN on both ends.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › eBGP Peering
eBGP Peering Steps
Step 1
Enable BGP with router bgp on both routers.
Step 2
Configure neighbor remote-as using the directly connected interface IP.
Step 3
Verify TCP 179 is allowed and that the neighbor reaches Established with show ip bgp summary.
Key Takeaway

Confirm remote-as and TCP reachability; use ebgp-multihop only when peers are not directly connected and you understand the TTL implications.

Concrete Config
! On Router A (R1) - AS 65001
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002
!
! On Router B (R2) - AS 65002
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote-as 65001
If neighbors are multiple hops apart, add ebgp-multihop on both sides with a hops value to raise the TTL for BGP packets.
Check: show ip bgp summary

screens.title: eBGP-Multihop and TTL Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes you need eBGP to work across more than one hop, for example when peering over an intermediate network or a tunnel. By default eBGP uses a TTL of 1 for BGP packets so that directly connected neighbors are expected. The ebgp-multihop command increases the TTL used for the BGP TCP connection, allowing the session to survive across intermediate routers. For instance, neighbor 192.168.1.2 ebgp-multihop 2 tells the router to set a TTL of 2 for BGP packets to that peer. A concrete example is peering over a GRE tunnel or across a transit network; ebgp-multihop lets you form the session without using loopbacks or other techniques. However, ebgp-multihop can be a trap if used carelessly: it makes BGP packets traverse other networks, so ensure intermediate devices permit TCP 179 and that you understand the security and routing implications. A common misconception is that ebgp-multihop replaces the need for proper neighbor configuration; it does not. You still need correct remote-as values and route reachability for the chosen source and destination IPs. Takeaway: use ebgp-multihop when necessary but pair it with verification of TCP reachability and clear security consideration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › eBGP Multihop
Why ebgp-multihop
Use when eBGP peers are not directly connected or when peering over a tunnel or transit segment.
Behavior
It increases the TTL used when forming the BGP TCP connection. Default eBGP TTL is 1.
Security and Reachability
Intermediate devices must allow TCP 179. Understand transit reachability before relying on multihop.
Key Takeaway

ebgp-multihop is a targeted tool to extend eBGP beyond direct neighbors; always verify edge-firewall and intermediate routing policies.

Example
neighbor 192.0.2.2 remote-as 65002
neighbor 192.0.2.2 ebgp-multihop 2
After configuring ebgp-multihop, confirm the session with show ip bgp summary and check that intermediate routers forward TCP 179.

screens.title: Configuring iBGP over Loopbacks
screens.narratorSegment: iBGP sessions are typically formed between routers within the same Autonomous System, and the recommended practice is to peer over loopback interfaces for stability. The key commands are neighbor remote-as and neighbor update-source Loopback0. update-source tells BGP to use the loopback interface’s IP as the source of the TCP connection, ensuring the peer sees the expected source address rather than a physical interface IP that may change. However, the loopback must be reachable via an IGP such as OSPF or static routes; without IGP reachability the session will not form. A concrete scenario: R1 has Loopback0 1.1.1.1 and R3 has Loopback0 3.3.3.3. Configure neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001 and neighbor 3.3.3.3 update-source Loopback0 on R1, then mirror on R3. A common misconception is that update-source alone is enough; in practice you must also ensure the underlying IGP advertises the loopbacks so the router can reach the neighbor’s loopback address. Key takeaway: pairing loopbacks with update-source and a functioning IGP gives resilient iBGP sessions across physical topology changes. Configuring iBGP over Loopbacks means use update-source loopback0 and ensure igp reachability so ibgp sessions remain stable even if physical links change.. In practical terms, using update-source and ensuring igp reachability to loopbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › iBGP over Loopbacks
Why loopbacks
Loopbacks provide a stable endpoint for BGP sessions; they are logical and remain up independent of physical interfaces.
Required IGP
An IGP must advertise reachability to each peer's loopback; otherwise the update-source pattern will fail to establish a TCP session.
Misconception
Some think update-source is optional; it is required when using loopbacks so the peer sees the expected source IP.
Key Takeaway

Combine update-source with a correct IGP to make iBGP over loopbacks robust against physical interface changes.

Concrete Config
! On R1 (AS 65001)
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 3.3.3.3 update-source Loopback0

! On R3 (AS 65001)
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 1.1.1.1 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 1.1.1.1 update-source Loopback0
Verify that OSPF or your IGP advertises loopbacks and that you can reach the peer's loopback address before expecting the BGP session to form.

screens.title: Advertising Networks with the network Command
screens.narratorSegment: The primary, most granular way to originate a prefix into BGP is the network command. This command advertises a prefix only if that exact prefix and mask exist in the router’s IP routing table. For example, network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0 will only be advertised if the router actually has a 10.0.0.0/24 route in its routing table — such as from a loopback address, an active interface, or a static route. If the routing table only lists 10.0.0.0/8, the /24 network command will not match and BGP will not advertise the /24. A common concrete solution is to configure a loopback or a static route to ensure the exact route exists, or to redistribute IGP routes into BGP when appropriate. Redistribution is an alternative but it is less granular and often injects many routes with an origin of incomplete, so use it with care. A frequent misconception is thinking network will announce any summarized or related route; it will not. Key takeaway: confirm an exact routing-table match before expecting BGP to advertise a network configured with the network command. Advertising Networks with the network Command means network <prefix> mask <mask> advertises a prefix only if an exact match appears in the local ip routing table.. In practical terms, exact-match requirement and practical ways to originate prefixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exact Match
keyIdea.text: network <prefix> mask <mask> advertises a prefix only if an exact match appears in the local IP routing table.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › network Command
How network works
network requires an exact prefix and mask present in the routing table to originate the route into BGP.
Example
interface Loopback1
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0

router bgp 65001
 network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0
If only 10.0.0.0/8 exists in the routing table, a network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0 will not match. Create the exact route or use a static route to null0 for summary advertisement if appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Always ensure the exact prefix/mask exists in the routing table before expecting network to originate it into BGP.

Redistribution alternative
You can redistribute an IGP into BGP, for example redistribute ospf 1, but this is less granular and can inject many routes unintentionally.
Use the network command for controlled advertisement; use redistribution when you intentionally want an entire IGP set in BGP and you manage filtering carefully.

screens.title: Network Command vs Redistribution
screens.narratorSegment: Both the network command and redistribution can inject routes into BGP, but they serve different operational needs. The network command is explicit and granular: it advertises only the specific prefix and mask you list, and only if that exact route exists in the IP routing table. This makes it ideal when you want full control over which prefixes appear in BGP. Redistribution takes many or all routes from another protocol, such as OSPF, and injects them into BGP. It is useful when you want whole sets of IGP-learned routes to be advertised quickly, but it is less precise and can accidentally send internal-only routes to external peers if not filtered. A concrete example: use network 192.168.100.0 mask 255.255.255.0 to advertise a single loopback prefix. Use redistribute ospf 1 only when you intentionally want your OSPF topology advertised into BGP and you are prepared to apply filtering. A common misconception is that redistribution is safer because it is automatic; in fact it can be more dangerous without proper route-maps or prefix-lists. Takeaway: prefer network for controlled advertisement and use redistribution only with careful filtering.

Use redistribute ospf 1 only when you intentionally want your OSPF topology advertised into BGP and you are prepared to apply filtering. A common misconception is that redistribution is safer because it is automatic; in fact it can be more dangerous without proper route-maps or prefix-lists. Takeaway: prefer network for controlled advertisement and use redistribution only with careful filtering.

keyIdea.title: Controlled vs Broad
keyIdea.text: Use network for precise advertisements and redistribution for broader injection, but always apply filters to avoid unintended leaks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Network vs Redistribution
Network Command
Precise, requires exact routing table entry.
router bgp 65001
 network 192.168.100.0 mask 255.255.255.0
Best for controlled advertisements and minimizing accidental leaks.
Redistribution
Broad, automatic injection of routes from another protocol.
router bgp 65001
 redistribute ospf 1
Use with route-maps or prefix-lists to filter what is injected. Mistake: redistributing everything into BGP without filters can leak internal-only routes.

screens.title: Hands-on Topology and Configuration Steps
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the hands-on activity described in the chapter. You will configure three routers: R1 (AS 65001), R2 (AS 65002), and R3 (AS 65001). Start by assigning IPs and loopbacks: create Loopback0 on R1 as 1.1.1.1/32 and on R3 as 3.3.3.3/32, and configure physical FastEthernet interfaces for connectivity between R1–R2 and R1–R3. Next, run OSPF on R1 and R3 to advertise their loopbacks and the link network so loopbacks reach each other; this ensures iBGP loopbacks are reachable. Then configure BGP: on R1 define neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002 for eBGP and neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001 with update-source Loopback0 for iBGP. On R2 configure its neighbor to R1 and advertise a dummy network with network 192.168.200.0 mask 255.255.255.0 after creating a loopback or static route for it. On R3 configure iBGP back to R1 and advertise its dummy network with the network command after ensuring the route exists. After configuration, verify with show ip bgp summary on each router and show ip bgp on R1 to see 192.168.200.0/24 and 192.168.100.0/24 learned. Common mistakes include forgetting update-source, missing IGP reachability, and network-command mismatches. Takeaway: follow the sequence—interfaces, IGP for loopbacks, BGP neighbors, then advertise networks and verify.

screens.title: Verifying BGP: Essential show Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is a critical step after configuration. The most important commands are show ip bgp summary, show ip bgp neighbors, show ip bgp, and show ip route bgp. show ip bgp summary gives a concise table of neighbor addresses, their ASN, session state, and the number of prefixes received — you want to see Established. show ip bgp neighbors provides session details, timers, message statistics, and the configured parameters for that peer; use it when debugging why a session did not form. show ip bgp lists the BGP routing table and path attributes for learned prefixes. Finally, show ip route bgp shows which BGP-learned routes have been installed in the global routing table. A concrete example: after forming eBGP between R1 and R2, run show ip bgp summary on both routers; if the neighbor state is Active, check TCP reachability and remote-as. To confirm what you are sending to a neighbor, run show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. A common misconception is that show ip bgp alone proves reachability; it shows learned routes but not whether they are installed in the IP routing table — use show ip route bgp for that. Takeaway: use this command set systematically to verify both the control plane and data plane outcomes of your BGP configuration.

Essential show commands

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common BGP Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting BGP often begins with simple checks that quickly reveal the root cause. If a neighbor stays in Active, first confirm TCP connectivity to port 179; an ACL or firewall commonly blocks BGP control traffic. Next, confirm the configured remote-as matches the neighbor’s ASN; a mismatch prevents progression to Established. For iBGP over loopbacks, check that update-source Loopback0 is configured on both sides and that an IGP advertises the loopback addresses so peers can reach them. When a network command does not cause a route to be advertised, verify that the exact prefix and mask exist in the local IP routing table — missing exact-match routes are the most frequent error. Also check for accidental summarization or a differing mask. A concrete diagnostic sequence: ping the neighbor IP, telnet to port 179 to confirm TCP, check show ip bgp neighbors for parameters, and inspect show ip route to find whether the required route exists. Misconception: people sometimes assume BGP will advertise any same-network block; it will not advertise a prefix unless it matches exactly. Takeaway: start with reachability and configuration symmetry checks, then inspect route presence and verification commands.

keyIdea.text: Check TCP 179 reachability, remote-as accuracy, update-source and IGP reachability for loopbacks, and exact routing-table matches for network commands.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Troubleshooting
Quick Diagnostic Steps
  1. Ping neighbor IP and test TCP to port 179.
  2. Confirm remote-as matches on both sides.
  3. For loopbacks, confirm update-source and IGP routes to loopbacks.
  4. Check show ip route for exact prefix/mask required by network command.
Concrete Example
If show ip bgp summary shows Active, try telnet 179 to see if the TCP handshake is allowed. If telnet fails, investigate ACLs or firewall rules. If telnet succeeds, confirm remote-as and check show ip bgp neighbors for mismatch or update-source issues.
Common Mistake

Assuming a network command advertises a prefix that only exists as a larger aggregate. Always confirm exact mask presence in the routing table.

screens.title: Avoiding Route Leaks — Filtering and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A critical operational safety practice is to never accidentally advertise internal-only or private prefixes to external eBGP peers. The chapter calls attention to the danger of sending RFC1918 ranges to the public internet. Before applying changes, always preview what a neighbor will receive using show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. Apply outbound filters such as prefix-lists, route-maps, or distribute-lists when speaking to eBGP peers to limit what you advertise. For example, ensure only legitimate public prefixes are permitted for eBGP sessions. A concrete workflow: decide which prefixes should be advertised, create a prefix-list that permits those prefixes and denies others, apply it outbound on your neighbor statement, and then confirm with the advertised-routes command. A common misconception is that a router will never accidentally leak private space; misconfigurations happen, and an inadvertent network or redistribution can cause widespread impact. Takeaway: build filters as part of every eBGP peer configuration and verify advertised routes before and after enabling a neighbor. Avoiding Route Leaks — Filtering and Best Practices means always use prefix-lists or route-maps to control ebgp outbound advertisements and verify advertised-routes before committing changes.. In practical terms, why you must filter ebgp advertisements and preview advertised routes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why filter
Prevent accidental advertisement of internal/private routes to eBGP peers which can cause route leaks and security issues.

screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts are the practical memory aids you should carry from this chapter. First, router bgp enables the BGP process and identifies your domain, but it does not advertise routes by itself. Second, neighbor remote-as is the core peer definition: for eBGP use directly connected IPs and for iBGP prefer loopbacks with update-source Loopback0, ensuring the IGP advertises those loopbacks. Third, the network mask command requires an exact match in the routing table; if the exact prefix and mask are not present, BGP will not advertise it. Each of these items maps directly to a command you will type and a verification step you should run. Keep these checks in mind when you configure and test so that sessions form reliably and only the intended prefixes are advertised. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical steps to bring BGP peering online and to advertise prefixes so routers exchange reachability information. We begin with the single global command that starts BGP — the router bgp command — and then configure both eBGP, which peers across different Autonomous Systems, and iBGP, which peers inside the same ASN using loopback addresses for stability. You will also learn the network command’s exact-match requirement for advertising prefixes and why an underlying route in the IP routing table matters. Finally, we cover the essential show commands you will run to verify neighbor state, seen prefixes, and what is advertised to each peer. These tasks matter because BGP is the control plane for exchanging routes between domains; small mistakes like a missing update-source or a wrong mask stop route propagation and can cause outages. As you move through the screens you’ll see configuration snippets and a step-by-step lab topology you can recreate in your simulator. Keep an eye on common mistakes such as blocked TCP port 179 and accidentally advertising private address space. By the end you should be able to form basic eBGP and iBGP sessions and verify their operation with confidence.

These objectives focus on the hands-on skills you will practice and the reasons they matter in production networks. First, you will configure basic eBGP peering between two directly connected routers in different Autonomous Systems — this demonstrates the neighbor remote-as pattern and the reliance on TCP port 179 for session establishment. Second, you will configure iBGP peering between routers in the same ASN using loopback interfaces and the update-source command; this gives greater session stability because loopbacks remain reachable as long as the IGP can route to them. Third, you will advertise network prefixes into BGP using the network command and learn the requirement that the exact prefix and mask must already exist in the router’s IP routing table — a common stumbling block for learners. Fourth, you will verify BGP neighbor status and route exchange using show ip bgp summary, show ip bgp, and show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. Each of these skills is practical: they let you bring up sessions reliably, avoid accidental route leakage, and confirm what your router sends and receives before you make irreversible changes.

Now we translate objectives into the exact actions you will take in the lab and on real routers. For eBGP you will enter router bgp with the local ASN and then add neighbor remote-as ; success requires TCP reachability to port 179 and matching remote-as on the far side. For iBGP you will configure neighbor loopback-ip remote-as local-as and add neighbor loopback-ip update-source Loopback0; this tells the router to source the TCP connection from the loopback address so peers recognize the expected source. When advertising networks, you will use network prefix mask netmask, but only after you ensure that prefix exists in the routing table — for example a loopback with an IP in that prefix or a static route pointing to null0 for summaries. For verification you will rely on show ip bgp summary to confirm Established state, show ip bgp to view the BGP table contents, and show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes to confirm what you are sending. Each of these steps reduces risk: proper sourcing, reachability, and verification prevent broken sessions and accidental route leaks.

The foundation of any BGP configuration is the simple global command router bgp followed by your Autonomous System Number, or ASN. This command tells the router to start the BGP process and to identify itself in BGP OPEN messages with that ASN. Think of the ASN like the administrative domain label: routers with different ASNs form eBGP sessions, while routers that share the same ASN form iBGP sessions. A concrete example is router bgp 65001 on R1 when R1 is managed as ASN 65001. That single command switches the device into BGP mode and lets you begin configuring neighbor relationships and route advertisements. A common misconception is that configuring router bgp alone advertises routes; it does not. You still must advertise specific prefixes or redistribute routes into BGP before those networks are shared with peers. Another subtle point is that ASNs must be correct on both ends of a peer relationship: a wrong remote-as prevents the session from ever reaching Established. Key takeaway: router bgp enables the process and identifies your domain. Always pair it with explicit neighbor definitions and verification steps so you know the process has established successfully.

Configuring eBGP is straightforward but requires precise addressing and the correct remote ASN. To form an eBGP session between directly connected routers you configure router bgp with your local ASN and then define neighbor remote-as. For example, on R1 in AS 65001 you add neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002; on R2 you add neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote-as 65001. BGP uses TCP port 179 to build the session; if TCP is blocked by an ACL or firewall the neighbor will stay in Active. Another important point: eBGP peers often use directly connected IP addresses for the neighbor statement, so underlying interface IP reachability is necessary. When peers are separated by multiple hops, ebgp-multihop can be used to increase TTL, for example neighbor 192.168.1.2 ebgp-multihop 2, but use this deliberately because it changes how BGP packets traverse the network. Concrete example: configure the neighbor commands on both routers, then verify with show ip bgp summary to see an Established session and the number of prefixes exchanged. Misconception to avoid: eBGP is not automatic when routers can ping each other; the neighbor remote-as must match and control-plane TCP must be allowed. Takeaway: set the correct remote-as and confirm TCP reachability before troubleshooting deeper.

Sometimes you need eBGP to work across more than one hop, for example when peering over an intermediate network or a tunnel. By default eBGP uses a TTL of 1 for BGP packets so that directly connected neighbors are expected. The ebgp-multihop command increases the TTL used for the BGP TCP connection, allowing the session to survive across intermediate routers. For instance, neighbor 192.168.1.2 ebgp-multihop 2 tells the router to set a TTL of 2 for BGP packets to that peer. A concrete example is peering over a GRE tunnel or across a transit network; ebgp-multihop lets you form the session without using loopbacks or other techniques. However, ebgp-multihop can be a trap if used carelessly: it makes BGP packets traverse other networks, so ensure intermediate devices permit TCP 179 and that you understand the security and routing implications. A common misconception is that ebgp-multihop replaces the need for proper neighbor configuration; it does not. You still need correct remote-as values and route reachability for the chosen source and destination IPs. Takeaway: use ebgp-multihop when necessary but pair it with verification of TCP reachability and clear security consideration.

iBGP sessions are typically formed between routers within the same Autonomous System, and the recommended practice is to peer over loopback interfaces for stability. The key commands are neighbor remote-as and neighbor update-source Loopback0. update-source tells BGP to use the loopback interface’s IP as the source of the TCP connection, ensuring the peer sees the expected source address rather than a physical interface IP that may change. However, the loopback must be reachable via an IGP such as OSPF or static routes; without IGP reachability the session will not form. A concrete scenario: R1 has Loopback0 1.1.1.1 and R3 has Loopback0 3.3.3.3. Configure neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001 and neighbor 3.3.3.3 update-source Loopback0 on R1, then mirror on R3. A common misconception is that update-source alone is enough; in practice you must also ensure the underlying IGP advertises the loopbacks so the router can reach the neighbor’s loopback address. Key takeaway: pairing loopbacks with update-source and a functioning IGP gives resilient iBGP sessions across physical topology changes. Configuring iBGP over Loopbacks means use update-source loopback0 and ensure igp reachability so ibgp sessions remain stable even if physical links change.. In practical terms, using update-source and ensuring igp reachability to loopbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The primary, most granular way to originate a prefix into BGP is the network command. This command advertises a prefix only if that exact prefix and mask exist in the router’s IP routing table. For example, network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0 will only be advertised if the router actually has a 10.0.0.0/24 route in its routing table — such as from a loopback address, an active interface, or a static route. If the routing table only lists 10.0.0.0/8, the /24 network command will not match and BGP will not advertise the /24. A common concrete solution is to configure a loopback or a static route to ensure the exact route exists, or to redistribute IGP routes into BGP when appropriate. Redistribution is an alternative but it is less granular and often injects many routes with an origin of incomplete, so use it with care. A frequent misconception is thinking network will announce any summarized or related route; it will not. Key takeaway: confirm an exact routing-table match before expecting BGP to advertise a network configured with the network command. Both the network command and redistribution can inject routes into BGP, but they serve different operational needs. The network command is explicit and granular: it advertises only the specific prefix and mask you list, and only if that exact route exists in the IP routing table. This makes it ideal when you want full control over which prefixes appear in BGP. Redistribution takes many or all routes from another protocol, such as OSPF, and injects them into BGP. It is useful when you want whole sets of IGP-learned routes to be advertised quickly, but it is less precise and can accidentally send internal-only routes to external peers if not filtered. A concrete example: use network 192.168.100.0 mask 255.255.255.0 to advertise a single loopback prefix. Use redistribute ospf 1 only when you intentionally want your OSPF topology advertised into BGP and you are prepared to apply filtering. A common misconception is that redistribution is safer because it is automatic; in fact it can be more dangerous without proper route-maps or prefix-lists. Takeaway: prefer network for controlled advertisement and use redistribution only with careful filtering.

This walkthrough follows the hands-on activity described in the chapter. You will configure three routers: R1 (AS 65001), R2 (AS 65002), and R3 (AS 65001). Start by assigning IPs and loopbacks: create Loopback0 on R1 as 1.1.1.1/32 and on R3 as 3.3.3.3/32, and configure physical FastEthernet interfaces for connectivity between R1–R2 and R1–R3. Next, run OSPF on R1 and R3 to advertise their loopbacks and the link network so loopbacks reach each other; this ensures iBGP loopbacks are reachable. Then configure BGP: on R1 define neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002 for eBGP and neighbor 3.3.3.3 remote-as 65001 with update-source Loopback0 for iBGP. On R2 configure its neighbor to R1 and advertise a dummy network with network 192.168.200.0 mask 255.255.255.0 after creating a loopback or static route for it. On R3 configure iBGP back to R1 and advertise its dummy network with the network command after ensuring the route exists. After configuration, verify with show ip bgp summary on each router and show ip bgp on R1 to see 192.168.200.0/24 and 192.168.100.0/24 learned. Common mistakes include forgetting update-source, missing IGP reachability, and network-command mismatches. Takeaway: follow the sequence—interfaces, IGP for loopbacks, BGP neighbors, then advertise networks and verify.

Verification is a critical step after configuration. The most important commands are show ip bgp summary, show ip bgp neighbors, show ip bgp, and show ip route bgp. show ip bgp summary gives a concise table of neighbor addresses, their ASN, session state, and the number of prefixes received — you want to see Established. show ip bgp neighbors provides session details, timers, message statistics, and the configured parameters for that peer; use it when debugging why a session did not form. show ip bgp lists the BGP routing table and path attributes for learned prefixes. Finally, show ip route bgp shows which BGP-learned routes have been installed in the global routing table. A concrete example: after forming eBGP between R1 and R2, run show ip bgp summary on both routers; if the neighbor state is Active, check TCP reachability and remote-as. To confirm what you are sending to a neighbor, run show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. A common misconception is that show ip bgp alone proves reachability; it shows learned routes but not whether they are installed in the IP routing table — use show ip route bgp for that. Takeaway: use this command set systematically to verify both the control plane and data plane outcomes of your BGP configuration.

Troubleshooting BGP often begins with simple checks that quickly reveal the root cause. If a neighbor stays in Active, first confirm TCP connectivity to port 179; an ACL or firewall commonly blocks BGP control traffic. Next, confirm the configured remote-as matches the neighbor’s ASN; a mismatch prevents progression to Established. For iBGP over loopbacks, check that update-source Loopback0 is configured on both sides and that an IGP advertises the loopback addresses so peers can reach them. When a network command does not cause a route to be advertised, verify that the exact prefix and mask exist in the local IP routing table — missing exact-match routes are the most frequent error. Also check for accidental summarization or a differing mask. A concrete diagnostic sequence: ping the neighbor IP, telnet to port 179 to confirm TCP, check show ip bgp neighbors for parameters, and inspect show ip route to find whether the required route exists. Misconception: people sometimes assume BGP will advertise any same-network block; it will not advertise a prefix unless it matches exactly. Takeaway: start with reachability and configuration symmetry checks, then inspect route presence and verification commands.

A critical operational safety practice is to never accidentally advertise internal-only or private prefixes to external eBGP peers. The chapter calls attention to the danger of sending RFC1918 ranges to the public internet. Before applying changes, always preview what a neighbor will receive using show ip bgp neighbors advertised-routes. Apply outbound filters such as prefix-lists, route-maps, or distribute-lists when speaking to eBGP peers to limit what you advertise. For example, ensure only legitimate public prefixes are permitted for eBGP sessions. A concrete workflow: decide which prefixes should be advertised, create a prefix-list that permits those prefixes and denies others, apply it outbound on your neighbor statement, and then confirm with the advertised-routes command. A common misconception is that a router will never accidentally leak private space; misconfigurations happen, and an inadvertent network or redistribution can cause widespread impact. Takeaway: build filters as part of every eBGP peer configuration and verify advertised routes before and after enabling a neighbor. These three concepts are the practical memory aids you should carry from this chapter. First, router bgp enables the BGP process and identifies your domain, but it does not advertise routes by itself. Second, neighbor remote-as is the core peer definition: for eBGP use directly connected IPs and for iBGP prefer loopbacks with update-source Loopback0, ensuring the IGP advertises those loopbacks. Third, the network mask command requires an exact match in the routing table; if the exact prefix and mask are not present, BGP will not advertise it. Each of these items maps directly to a command you will type and a verification step you should run. Keep these checks in mind when you configure and test so that sessions form reliably and only the intended prefixes are advertised.
